finding.title: UnixFileLock follows symlinks and truncates arbitrary files via O_TRUNC
finding.evidence: Attacker-influenced input is the lock file path stored in self._context.lock_file (BaseFileLock.lock_file / constructor lock_file). Reachable flow: BaseFileLock.acquire() (filelock/_api.py:332 -> self._acquire()) calls UnixFileLock._acquire(), which builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41, adding O_CREAT only when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is False) and then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) (line 44). The open call has no O_NOFOLLOW, and Path(self.lock_file).exists() follows symlinks, so a symlink planted at the lock-file path is transparently followed and O_TRUNC truncates whatever it points at (then fcntl.flock locks that target). No validation rejects symlinks, and raise_on_not_writable_file/ensure_directory_exists also follow links. Consequence: when the lock path lives in a directory the attacker can write (e.g. a shared /tmp or attacker-controlled project dir), an attacker creates a symlink named after the lock file pointing at a victim file writable by the process, causing arbitrary file truncation/data destruction on the next lock acquisition. The corresponding fixed release in the same tree (filelock-3.20.3) adds O_NOFOLLOW to this exact os.open call, confirming the missing link-following protection is the root cause.

finding.title: WindowsFileLock follows reparse points/junctions and truncates arbitrary files
finding.evidence: WindowsFileLock._acquire() opens the lock path with flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC (lines 22-26) via os.open(self.lock_file, flags, self._context.mode) (line 28) and then locks it with msvcrt.locking. There is no check that the path is a reparse point (symlink/junction); raise_on_not_writable_file (line 20) and ensure_directory_exists (line 21) likewise operate through links. An attacker who can create a directory junction or symlink at the lock path (e.g. in a shared/user-writable directory) redirects the O_CREAT|O_TRUNC write to an arbitrary file, truncating it and holding the lock on the wrong file. The fixed release present in the same extraction adds a _is_reparse_point() guard using GetFileAttributesW before opening, confirming the missing reparse-point/link-following protection is the root cause.

finding.title: Lock file opened with O_TRUNC following symlinks (arbitrary file truncation/chmod)
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (adding O_CREAT when the path is absent) and calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44 with no O_NOFOLLOW and no prior lstat/ownership check. Because O_TRUNC is honored after link resolution, if a local attacker can place a symlink at the lock-file path (predictable lock paths in shared/world-writable directories such as /tmp), the process follows it, truncates the symlink target, and then runs os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode) at line 46, resetting the target's permissions to 0o644. The fcntl.flock at line 48 performs no validation of the resolved inode, so the destructive open/fchmod happen before any lock ownership is established. SoftFileLock is unaffected because its O_CREAT|O_EXCL open fails with EEXIST on an existing symlink, confirming the defect is specific to this O_TRUNC open.

finding.title: Verifier cache ignores exp when iat is absent, accepting expired JWTs
finding.evidence: In cacheSet, the entire time-range computation (including the exp deadline at lines 95-100) is gated by `if (hasIat)` at line 92, where `hasIat = payload && typeof payload.iat === 'number'` (line 89). JWT `iat` is optional, so for a valid token that has `exp` but no `iat`, cacheValue[2] is never set from `exp`; line 106 then falls back to `maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL` (line 105, default cacheTTL = 600_000 ms, line 384). On later lookups the cache is consulted before decoding/verifying (`cache.get(cacheKeyBuilder(token))` at line 258) and a hit is returned at lines 262-271 without ever calling verifyToken, whose expiration validator (lines 452-459, 164-171) is the only place `exp` is rechecked. Thus an attacker who possesses any valid token containing `exp` but no `iat`, verified once while still valid with the `cache` option enabled, can replay that exact token and have it accepted up to cacheTTL past its real expiration (GHSA-x937-hj6v-793p / CVE-2026-107719, fixed in 6.3.4 by deriving the cache deadline from `exp` independently of `iat`).

finding.title: Panic during element drop in ThinVec::clear leaves stale length, causing double-drop/double-free on unwind
finding.evidence: clear() (src/lib.rs:1082-1087) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 and only then calls `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085. If any element's `Drop` unwinds (safe Rust, e.g. a destructor that panics on attacker-controlled data), the length is never reset; the panic propagates to a caller that catches it (std::panic::catch_unwind) while the ThinVec is still alive with its original `len`. When that ThinVec is later dropped (or read, e.g. as_slice), Drop for ThinVec (src/lib.rs:1910-1930) calls drop_in_place(&mut this[..]) over the same elements again, so each already-destroyed element is dropped a second time (use-after-free/double-free of any heap allocation owned by T). This is exactly the panic-safety fix added upstream in thin-vec 0.2.16 (a DropGuard that resets len during unwind), which is absent here. Configuration is default (gecko-ffi off; the non-gecko clear at line 1082 is always compiled). PoC executed with rustc/cargo (stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu) against this exact source: a 3-element ThinVec<Bomb> with a panicking Drop inside catch_unwind produced drops_after_clear=3, and dropping the vector afterwards raised the total to 6 drops for 3 elements (sound behavior would be 3), i.e. every element was destroyed twice.

finding.title: Panic during element drop in IntoIter::drop double-drops remaining elements
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop (src/lib.rs:2539-2556) moves the vector into a local (`mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` at 2546), then destroys the remaining elements with `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` at line 2547, and only afterwards clears the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` at line 2548. If any element Drop unwinds, the `vec` local is itself dropped during unwinding (its ThinVec::drop at 1910-1930 runs drop_in_place over the full, unchanged length), destroying the already-destroyed elements again. Because this.vec was replaced with an empty ThinVec, the standard leak-amplification guard that normally protects Drain is bypassed, so the double-drop is unconditional once a destructor panics. Safe-Rust/attacker-reachable: create ThinVec<T> whose T::drop can panic, wrap v.into_iter() (or its drop) in catch_unwind, and consume part of the iterator; the panic during the iterator's drop corrupts the heap via the second drop. The upstream 0.2.16 fix that installs a DropGuard resetting len during unwind is absent. Default configuration (gecko-ffi off). PoC executed against this exact source: IntoIter over 3 elements consumed once (2 remaining) then dropped inside catch_unwind produced 6 element drops instead of the expected 2, demonstrating the double-drop/UAF.

finding.title: Double free in ThinVec::clear when an element Drop panics
finding.evidence: ThinVec::clear calls ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..]) at line 1084 and only resets the logical length on the following line with self.set_len(0). If any element's Drop::drop panics, unwinding skips line 1085, leaving the ThinVec length unchanged while some elements were already destroyed. When the container is later dropped (for example after panic::catch_unwind), Drop for ThinVec calls ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..]) again and double-drops/frees the same elements, giving an attacker-controlled double-free/use-after-free primitive. No DropGuard ensures the length reset during unwinding.

finding.title: Double free in IntoIter::drop when an element Drop panics
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop's helper transfers the backing ThinVec into the local variable vec via mem::replace at line 2546, then at line 2547 calls ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]) for the unconsumed suffix. If an element's Drop::drop panics during that call, the following line vec.set_len_non_singleton(0) is skipped. During unwinding the local vec is dropped with its original length, so Drop for ThinVec drops the same elements again (including already-dropped ones), producing a double free/use-after-free. The implementation omits the DropGuard pattern that std::vec::IntoIter uses to zero the length on panic.

finding.title: Empty HMAC secret from async key resolver yields forged-signature acceptance
finding.evidence: In the async path, getAsyncKey returns the app's key at line 319; a resolver that returns '' is converted to a zero-length Buffer at lines 326-327 (no emptiness error), then line 350 calls prepareKeyOrSecret, whose line 36 builds createSecretKey(<empty buffer>) without any empty-secret check (the later fix added ensureSecretIsNotEmpty here). verifyToken then sees a truthy KeyObject (hasKey=true at line 180) and enforces the signature, but verifySignature at line 139 computes HMAC with the empty key. Because the empty secret is publicly known, an attacker computes createHmac('SHA256','') over header.payload and submits alg HS256 with that signature; the token verifies and all claim validators run against attacker-chosen claims, giving full authentication bypass whenever the resolver can return an empty string (e.g. unknown kid/tenant).

finding.title: createVerifier accepts unsigned JWTs when key is '' or null and algorithms is set
finding.evidence: createVerifier only checks the key type (lines 391-397) and skips detection/preparation for any falsy key via `if (key && keyType !== 'function')` at line 399, so an app calling createVerifier({ algorithms: ['HS256'], key: '' }) (or key:null) leaves allowedAlgorithms populated while no key is materialized. At verifyToken, hasKey is false (line 180); a token ending with '.' has signature === '' so neither branch at lines 182-186 throws (no key and no signature), and validateAlgorithmAndSignature line 139 skips verifySignature because `signature` is falsy, while line 134 accepts header.alg present in the explicit allowlist. An attacker therefore submits an unsigned token whose header alg is in the allowlist and whose exp/nbf/aud claims are attacker-chosen; it is accepted with no cryptographic verification.

finding.title: Attacker-controlled claim values run through unguarded application RegExp (ReDoS)
finding.evidence: ensureStringClaimMatcher returns any configured matcher object that has a .test method verbatim (lines 47-48), i.e. application-supplied RegExp objects for allowedJti/allowedAud/allowedIss/allowedSub/allowedNonce are stored as-is. validateClaimValues then executes a.test(v) at line 159 with v taken from the token payload (line 210). A token is fully attacker-controlled, so a value crafted to trigger catastrophic backtracking in a configured pattern (e.g. /^(a+)+$/) causes unbounded CPU inside the regex engine during verification; a single request can pin the event loop (CPU-exhaustion DoS). The library performs no complexity analysis of the RegExp and does not reset lastIndex, so a stateful /g or /y matcher also gives non-deterministic allowed/rejected results.

finding.title: Verifier cache accepts expired tokens that lack an iat claim
finding.evidence: cacheSet only records the token's time bounds when the payload has a numeric iat (line 89). For a signed token that carries exp but no iat, the exp branch at lines 95-101 is skipped, so cacheValue[2] stays 0 and line 106 replaces it with maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL (default 600000 ms) instead of exp. Subsequent verify calls hit the cache condition at lines 262-268 (`max === 0 || now <= max`), so the successful result is returned for the whole cacheTTL window without re-running the exp validator. With caching enabled, an attacker (or any legitimate short-lived token holder) can keep presenting a token with exp already in the past and it continues to be accepted until the cache entry expires, extending authorization past the token's stated lifetime.

finding.title: Attacker-controlled BLAKE2b key length overflows fixed 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b(msg, key) passes the caller-supplied key and its unbounded length straight through: line 277 key=b'' if key is None else key, line 281 crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)). Blake2b.__init__ does the same at line 297 (crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key))). In monocypher.c:638-646 crypto_blake2b_keyed calls crypto_blake2b_keyed_init, which at monocypher.c:544-546 executes 'u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);' where COPY is a byte-by-byte loop (monocypher.c:65) that copies key_size bytes with no upper bound. The BLAKE2b specification allows at most 64 key bytes, but no length validation exists anywhere in the binding or the called function. An attacker who can supply the key (e.g. monocypher.blake2b(b'data', key=b'A'*200) or Blake2b(key=b'A'*200)) causes up to len(key) bytes to be written past the 128-byte stack buffer, corrupting the saved stack frame / return address with attacker-influenced data, i.e. a stack buffer overflow with RCE potential. A key of length 64 is safe, while >128 overflows.

finding.title: Missing length validation for fixed-size key/nonce/secret buffers causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: Several bindings forward Python objects to C parameters declared as fixed-size arrays and never validate their length. In lock(), line 181 crypto_aead_lock(crypto_text, mac, key, nonce, associated_data, len(associated_data), message, len(message)) passes key and nonce unchecked, while the C declaration is 'crypto_aead_lock(u8 *cipher_text, u8 mac[16], const u8 key[32], const u8 nonce[24], ...)' (monocypher.c:2931) and the body reads all 32 key bytes and 24 nonce bytes unconditionally. Cython converts a Python bytes object to a raw pointer with no size check, so monocypher.lock(b'short', b'short', b'msg') makes the library read past the end of the key/nonce buffers. The same root cause (no validation of fixed-size array inputs) affects unlock (line 199 key[32]/nonce[24]/mac[16]), chacha20 (lines 267/269 read key[32] although only the nonce length is checked at 266/268), compute_key_exchange_public_key (line 362 secret_key[32]), key_exchange (line 375 both 32-byte keys), and signature_check (line 429 signature[64]/public_key[32]). Reading heap memory beyond a short input leaks adjacent data into cryptographic computation/verification and can fault past a page boundary, giving an availability and limited information-disclosure impact.

finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks undersizes argon2 work area, causing heap buffer overflow
finding.evidence: argon2i_32(nb_blocks, ...) copies the caller-supplied nb_blocks straight into config.nb_blocks (line 328) with no minimum check, then allocates work_area = malloc(nb_blocks * 1024) (line 345) and calls crypto_argon2(hash, ..., work_area, config, ...) (line 347). Monocypher requires nb_blocks >= 8; in monocypher.c crypto_argon2 computes lane_size = (config.nb_blocks/4)*4, so for nb_blocks in {0,1} lane_size becomes 0, yet the initial fill loop unconditionally writes two 1024-byte blocks: 'blocks[l*lane_size + i]' for i=0..1 (monocypher.c:777-781). The work area is only nb_blocks*1024 bytes (1024 or 0 bytes), so the second block write overruns the heap allocation; for nb_blocks in {2,3} the later 'last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1' = blocks-1 produces an out-of-bounds read. PoC: pymonocypher.argon2i_32(1, 1, b'pw', b'salt'). No length/bounds validation exists on nb_blocks between line 328 and the call.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc result passed to crypto_argon2 causes NULL pointer dereference
finding.evidence: work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024)) (line 345) is used without checking for NULL at the crypto_argon2(hash, ..., work_area, ...) call (line 347). nb_blocks is attacker-controlled and only bounded by the uint32_t assignment at line 328, so up to 0xffffffff blocks (~4 TiB) can be requested. When malloc fails and returns NULL, crypto_argon2 immediately writes in-bounds references such as blocks[l*lane_size + i] (monocypher.c:781) and the final ZERO(p, 128*nb_blocks) (monocypher.c:915), dereferencing NULL and crashing the process.

finding.title: Unvalidated Blake2b key length overflows fixed 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: Blake2b.__init__ passes key = b'' if key is None else key with len(key) as the key size directly to crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key)) (line 297); the module-level blake2b() does the same at line 281. In monocypher.c crypto_blake2b_keyed_init performs 'u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);' where COPY is an unbounded element-by-element loop (monocypher.c:65,545-547). Monocypher expects key_size <= 64, but nothing validates it, so any key longer than 128 bytes written by the caller (for example pymonocypher.Blake2b(key=b'A'*1000) or pymonocypher.blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*1000)) overflows the 128-byte stack buffer and corrupts the stack.

finding.title: Fixed-size key/nonce parameters read out of bounds for short Python buffers
finding.evidence: lock() forwards caller-provided key and nonce straight to crypto_aead_lock(crypto_text, mac, key, nonce, ...) (line 181) without validating their lengths, and crypto_aead_init_x unconditionally copies 32 key bytes and 24 nonce bytes (monocypher.c:2870-2876). Cython lowers the extern 'const uint8_t key[32]'/'const uint8_t nonce[24]' declarations to raw pointers with no size check, so passing a shorter bytes object (e.g. pymonocypher.lock(b'k', b'n', b'msg')) makes the C code read past the Python buffer. The same missing-validation pattern reaches other fixed-array sinks: unlock at line 199, chacha20 at lines 267/269 (32-byte key), key_exchange at line 375 (32-byte your_secret_key/their_public_key) and signature_check at line 429 (64-byte signature and 32-byte public_key). These out-of-bounds reads leak adjacent heap contents through the derived outputs and can crash the process, unlike the sibling functions elligator_map (line 501) and elligator_rev (line 519), which do bounds-check their inputs.

finding.title: Double free when an element Drop panics during ThinVec::clear
finding.evidence: `ThinVec::clear` (lines 1082-1087) executes `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 and only afterwards resets the length with `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085. If any element's `Drop` unwinds, line 1085 is skipped and the header keeps the old `len` even though those elements were already dropped. The subsequent `ThinVec::drop` (line 1917 `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) then drops the same elements a second time, freeing their resources twice (double free / use-after-free). This is reachable from purely safe code: `let mut v = thin_vec![D, D, D]; let _ = catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(|| v.clear())); drop(v);` where `D::drop` panics once. Fixed upstream in 0.2.16 by wrapping the drop in a guard that always calls `set_len(0)`.

finding.title: Double free when an element Drop panics while dropping IntoIter
finding.evidence: In `impl Drop for IntoIter`, `drop_non_singleton` (lines 2544-2550) calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` at line 2547 before zeroing the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` at line 2548. If an element's `Drop` unwinds, unwinding drops the local `vec`, whose header still holds the old length, so `ThinVec::drop` (line 1917) drops the already-dropped tail again, producing a double free. Reachable from safe code: make `v: ThinVec<D>`, then `let mut it = v.into_iter(); it.next();` and drop `it` with an element whose `Drop` panics. Fixed upstream in 0.2.16 by using a DropGuard that zeroes the length on unwind.

finding.title: Unchecked invalid Layout when size overflows isize::MAX after rounding to alignment
finding.evidence: `layout::<T>` builds the allocation layout with `Layout::from_size_align_unchecked(alloc_size::<T>(cap), alloc_align::<T>())` at line 441. `alloc_size` (lines 386-410) only rejects `final_size > isize::MAX`, but the `Layout` invariant additionally requires that the size, rounded up to `align`, must not exceed `isize::MAX`. For a type whose `alloc_align` is 8 (e.g. `u8`) and `cap = isize::MAX - 16`, `alloc_size` returns exactly `isize::MAX`, so an invalid `Layout` is created and passed to `alloc`/`handle_alloc_error` (lines 452-457), which is undefined behavior. Reachable from safe `ThinVec::<u8>::with_capacity(isize::MAX as usize - 16)`. Fixed upstream in 0.2.19 by using checked `Layout::from_size_align(..).ok().unwrap_cap_overflow()`.

finding.title: gecko-ffi reallocate zeroes length when migrating an inline (auto) array
finding.evidence: In gecko-ffi mode `reallocate` copies the inline elements into `new_header` (lines 1763-1768) but then only zeroes the *old* header's length via `self.set_len_non_singleton(0)` at line 1769; the freshly allocated `new_header` still has `len = 0` from `header_with_capacity`, and `self.ptr` is switched to it at line 1772. Thus a `reserve`/`push` on a non-empty `AutoThinVec` silently resets `len` to 0, leaving the copied elements unreachable so they are never dropped (memory leak / data loss). Fixed upstream in 0.2.16 by adding `new_header.as_mut().set_len(len)` after the copy.

finding.title: Heap buffer overflow in argon2i_32: nb_blocks is used without the required size validation
finding.evidence: arg2 'nb_blocks' is caller-controlled and is copied straight into the Argon2 config at line 328 ('config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks') with no lower-bound/consistency check, while line 345 allocates the work area as malloc(nb_blocks * 1024) and line 347 hands that pointer to monocypher's crypto_argon2(). Monocypher computes segment_size = nb_blocks/nb_lanes/4 and lane_size = segment_size*4 (monocypher.c:752-754) and unconditionally writes the first two 1024-byte blocks of every lane, i.e. blocks[0] and blocks[1] = 2048 bytes, in its 'fill first 2 blocks of each lane' loop (monocypher.c:776-783). For nb_blocks < 4 (nb_lanes is hard-coded to 1 at line 330) segment_size/lane_size round down to 0, so those two block writes always target blocks[0]/blocks[1] no matter how large the allocation is: argon2i_32(1, 3, b'p', b's') allocates only 1024 bytes and the library writes 2048 bytes, overflowing the heap chunk and corrupting adjacent heap metadata/objects (no other check protects this call; only the unrelated _validate_u32 length checks on password/salt/key/ad run). Monocypher's API contract requires nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes; this binding never enforces it, which is why upstream added 'if config.nb_blocks < (config.nb_lanes * 8): raise ValueError(...)' in 4.0.2.8 (GHSA-8f95-v3jq-cj86 / CVE-2026-53720, CWE-122/CWE-787/CWE-1284) for exactly this function.

finding.title: ItemAtIndex index validity check is bypassable, decoupling sha.circom output from the compression array
finding.evidence: Attacker input: the public `paddedInLength` of `Sha256Bytes`/`Sha256BytesPartial` (sha.circom:19/50) or of `Sha256General`/`Sha256Partial` (sha.circom:97/219). Flow: sha.circom:110-111 (and 233-234) sets `inBlockIndex = paddedInLength >> 9` with the constraint `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512`, so `paddedInLength = 0` is an accepted witness and yields `inBlockIndex = 0`. That value is then used as the selector index at sha.circom:195 (and 292): `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1`, which is `-1` (i.e. p-1 as a field element). Unsafe sink: `ItemAtIndex` in array.circom:15-46 only guards the index with `component lessThan = LessThan(bitLength); lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1;` (array.circom:25-28) and then emits `out <== calcTotal.sum` (array.circom:45, reached from sha.circom:196/293). Failed protection: `LessThan(n)` from circomlib does not range-check `in[0]`; it only constrains `in[0] + 2^n - in[1]` to fit in n+1 bits. For `index = p-1` this expression equals `2^n - maxArrayLen - 1`, a small positive value whose bit n is 0, so `lessThan.out` evaluates to 1 and the `=== 1` guard is satisfied even though `index` is out of [0, maxArrayLen). Because no `IsEqual` in array.circom:34-42 matches p-1, `calcTotal.sum` is 0, so every selector output `arraySelectors[k].out` (and hence every bit of the circuit output `out[256]`) is forced to 0. The robust alternative (asserting `calcTotalIndex.sum === 1`, present in later upstream revisions but absent here) is missing, so the output is not constrained to be a genuine selected compression result. Required configuration: any instantiation, e.g. `Sha256Bytes(maxByteLength)` with maxByteLength a multiple of 64. Net effect: a malicious prover can satisfy the circuit while claiming SHA256(msg) = 0^256 for an arbitrary padded message, i.e. a soundness break of the hash circuit.

finding.title: UnixFileLock follows symlinks at the lock path, letting an attacker truncate or create arbitrary files
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41) and only adds os.O_CREAT when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is False (lines 42-43), then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44 without os.O_NOFOLLOW. Because the lock file path is opened by following links, an attacker who can write to the directory that holds the lock file (a very common setup, e.g. a world-writable /tmp cache/state directory used by a more privileged process) can pre-create lock_file as a symlink pointing at a victim such as /root/.ssh/authorized_keys or an /etc configuration file. os.open then resolves the link and the O_TRUNC flag silently zeroes the victim file; if instead the attacker leaves a dangling symlink, exists() returns False, O_CREAT is added, and os.open creates a file at the attacker-chosen target location. Nothing on this path sets O_NOFOLLOW and raise_on_not_writable_file is never invoked here, so the write-permission check that SoftFileLock/W indowsFileLock perform does not apply. SoftFileLock is not affected because it uses O_CREAT|O_EXCL (filelock/_soft.py:20-27), which refuses to open through an existing link, confirming the Unix implementation is the vulnerable one.

finding.title: Bad-debt settlement health check mixes unscaled deposit with WAD instead of bucket scale
finding.evidence: In `_forgiveBadDebt`, the HPB bad-debt path loads `unscaledDeposit = Deposits.unscaledValueAt(deposits_, index)` (line 456) and `depositRemaining = unscaledDeposit - depositUsed` (line 467), so `depositRemaining` is an unscaled Fenwick amount; the correct scaled conversion is already used at line 457 (`Maths.wmul(scale, unscaledDeposit)`) with `scale` returned by `Deposits.findIndexAndSumOfSum` at line 455. The bucket-bankruptcy test at line 486 instead multiplies the unscaled value by `Maths.WAD` (`depositRemaining * Maths.WAD + hpbBucket.collateral * _priceAt(index) <= bucketLP`), so for any pool whose quote-token scale differs from 1e18 the comparison against `hpbBucket.lps` is wrong each time an attacker calls `settle()` on a kicked loan whose bad debt reaches the HPB (entered whenever `vars.unscaledDeposit != 0`, line 353). Buckets whose remaining deposit and collateral still back outstanding LP get marked bankrupt (`hpbBucket.lps = 0`, `bankruptcyTime = block.timestamp`, lines 488-489) destroying lender LP, or genuinely unbacked buckets are not bankrupted. Upstream fixed this by comparing against `scale` (commit 03d255d7, PR #971).

finding.title: Uncapped t0RepayAmount underflows borrower t0Debt in bucketTake
finding.evidence: `borrower.t0Debt = vars.t0BorrowerDebt - vars.t0RepayAmount` (line 168 in `bucketTake`; the identical subtraction is at line 242 in `take`) computes remaining borrower debt from `vars.t0RepayAmount` produced by `_calculateTakeFlowsAndBondChange` (invoked at line 446 with the bucket's price/deposit), which is not bounded by the borrower's t0 debt. Any taker can call `bucketTake`/`take` on an auction where the deposit/take flow repays more t0 debt than the borrower owes; Solidity 0.8 panics on the underflow, so the take reverts and the liquidation cannot be completed, and the same unvalidated value is added/subtracted from `poolState_.t0Debt` (lines 170-171). Upstream added `vars.t0RepayAmount = Maths.min(vars.t0RepayAmount, vars.t0BorrowerDebt)` (commit c13ae9b2, PR #1033).

finding.title: Bucket take prices the bond penalty factor with the auction price instead of the bucket price
finding.evidence: `_takeBucket` calls `_prepareTake(liquidation, borrower_.t0Debt, borrower_.collateral, params_.inflator)` at line 424, i.e. without the bucket price, and the bucket price is only read afterwards at line 436 (`vars_.bucketPrice = _priceAt(params_.index)`). `_prepareTake` therefore computes `vars.bpf = _bpf(borrowerDebt, collateral, neutralPrice, bondFactor, vars.auctionPrice)` from the auction price, and this BPF drives `vars.factor` and the bond change/kicker reward applied in `_rewardBucketTake` (lines 456-464) even though the taker pays the bucket price bound at line 439/442. A taker or kicker can therefore choose `index_`/`depositTake_` such that the kicker bond reward/penalty (`bondChange`, `isRewarded`) is computed against a different price than the transfer, mispricing the bond. Upstream passes the bucket price into `_prepareTake` and uses it for `_bpf` (commit 12e69802, PR #970).

finding.title: lenderKick updates interest rate with a LUP that no longer matches pool debt
finding.evidence: `lenderKick()` calls `_updateInterestState(poolState, result.lup)` at line 371 using the LUP returned by `KickerActions.lenderKick`, which was computed before the kick moved the borrower's debt into the auction accumulators at line 356 (`poolState.t0DebtInAuction += result.t0KickedDebt`, followed by writing `poolBalances.t0DebtInAuction` at line 368). `_updateInterestState` feeds that stale price into the EMA/interest-rate and debt-to-collateral update for the post-kick pool debt, so any kicker/lender can push the pool interest rate to a value inconsistent with the actual market state. Upstream replaced it with a freshly computed LUP, `_updateInterestState(poolState, Deposits.getLup(deposits, poolState.debt))` (commit dc66b009, PR #972).

finding.title: Lock-file open follows symlinks (no O_NOFOLLOW), enabling arbitrary file truncation/permission rewrite
finding.evidence: The target package is byte-identical to upstream filelock 3.20.0 (verified by diffing against the 3.13.1/3.16.1/3.18.0/3.20.0 sdist trees; no other differences). In UnixFileLock._acquire, open_flags is built at line 41 as `os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC` (plus O_CREAT only when Path.exists() is false, lines 42-43), then line 44 calls `os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode)` with no O_NOFOLLOW, and line 46 calls `os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode)`. An attacker who can write the directory holding the lock path replaces the expected lock file with a symlink to a victim file. The Path.exists() check at line 42 resolves the target and does not reject a symlink, and unlike WindowsFileLock/SoftFileLock this method never calls raise_on_not_writable_file, so there is no pre-check mitigation. When a privileged application later calls FileLock(path).acquire(), os.open follows the symlink and O_TRUNC zeroes the victim file, and os.fchmod rewrites its mode to the lock mode (0o644): arbitrary integrity/availability loss on files the victim can write. Sibling sinks share the same root cause: SoftFileLock._acquire opens with `os.open(self.lock_file, flags, ...)` at filelock/_soft.py line 27 without O_NOFOLLOW, and WindowsFileLock._acquire opens `os.open(self.lock_file, flags, ...)` at filelock/_windows.py line 28 without any reparse-point/junction check (msvcrt.locking then applies to the followed target). Upstream fixed exactly this in 3.20.1/3.20.3 by adding `open_flags |= getattr(os,'O_NOFOLLOW',0)` in _unix.py/_soft.py and adding GetFileAttributesW reparse-point detection in _windows.py; the audited 3.20.0 tree lacks all of these protections. A local reproduction script was written but symlink creation was blocked by the audit host (WinError 1314), so no PoC execution is claimed; the finding rests on inspected source plus the upstream security-fix diff.

finding.title: UnixFileLock follows a symlink at the lock path and truncates/chmods an arbitrary victim file (TOCTOU)
finding.evidence: _acquire builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41), tests Path(self.lock_file).exists() (line 42) and then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, mode) at line 44 with no O_NOFOLLOW. lock_file is the caller-supplied path and is typically predictable (e.g. a shared/temp dir), so an attacker with create permission in that directory can unlink the lock and plant a symlink to a victim file in the window between the exists() check and the open. The kernel follows the link, O_TRUNC zeroes the target, and the following os.fchmod(fd, mode) at line 46 rewrites its permissions; the symlink is treated as the lock so no error surfaces. Fixed in 3.20.1 by adding O_NOFOLLOW (CVE-2025-68146).

finding.title: WindowsFileLock follows a symlink/junction at the lock path and truncates an arbitrary victim file (TOCTOU)
finding.evidence: _acquire only stats the path via raise_on_not_writable_file (line 20), builds flags os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREAT|os.O_TRUNC (lines 22-26) and calls os.open(self.lock_file, flags, mode) at line 28 without rejecting reparse points. With symlink/junction creation rights (Developer Mode on Windows 10+), an attacker replaces the predictable lock path with a reparse point during the check-to-open window; os.open follows it and O_TRUNC truncates the victim target. Fixed in 3.20.1 by a GetFileAttributesW reparse-point check (CVE-2025-68146).

finding.title: SoftFileLock TOCTOU between writability check and open lets a symlink at the lock path break/DoS locking
finding.evidence: _acquire validates writability with raise_on_not_writable_file(self.lock_file) at line 17 (which follows symlinks through os.stat in _util.py) and only later calls os.open(self.lock_file, flags, mode) at line 27 (O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_TRUNC) with no O_NOFOLLOW. An attacker able to create names in the lock directory can win the race between line 17 and line 27 by placing a symlink at the lock path; the resulting open error is misclassified by the except block (only EEXIST is swallowed), so the lock silently fails to be acquired and processes no longer serialize on the resource (silent lock-acquisition failure / denial of service on attacker-controlled target). Fixed in 3.20.3 by adding O_NOFOLLOW (CVE-2026-22701, CWE-362/367/59).

finding.title: Empty/null key silently disables signature verification, accepting forged unsigned tokens
finding.evidence: verify() flows attacker token -> decode() -> verifyToken(). In verifyToken the guard `hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key` (line 180) is false when the configured key is an empty string or null, and the check `if (hasKey && !signature) throw missingSignature` (line 182) is skipped. validateAlgorithmAndSignature then runs `if (signature && !verifySignature(...))` (line 139): an empty signature is falsy, so verifySignature is never called and no signature failure can occur. createVerifier's config validation at line 399 only performs key detection when `key && keyType !== 'function'`, so `key: ''` (typeof 'string') or `key: null` (typeof 'object') pass validation with no rejection (older /tmp/.tmp2f4iOo snapshot lacks the fix that throws 'The key option is required unless the only allowed algorithm is "none"'). When an algorithm allowlist is supplied, `allowedAlgorithms.includes(header.alg)` (line 134) is satisfied, so `alg` from the attacker header passes and nothing else is verified. PoC (src/index.js of the audit root): createVerifier({key:'', algorithms:['HS256']}) accepted the crafted token `b64({alg:'HS256',typ:'JWT'}).b64({sub:'attacker',admin:true}).` (trailing dot => empty signature) and returned {"sub":"attacker","admin":true}; the control verifier with key 'a-real-secret' correctly rejected the same token with FAST_JWT_MISSING_SIGNATURE. Any deployment using an empty/env-unset/null key together with an explicit algorithm list is fully authentication-bypassed.

finding.title: Cached verification ignores exp when iat is absent, keeping expired tokens valid
finding.evidence: cacheSet() only computes the expiration bound inside `if (hasIat)` (line 92), where hasIat = `payload && typeof payload.iat === 'number'` (line 89). For a correctly signed token that has exp but no iat, the block at lines 95-100 that sets cacheValue[2] to payload.exp*1000 is skipped; cacheValue[2] then collapses to maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL (lines 105-106). On subsequent calls verify()'s cache-hit test (lines 262-269) sees min===0 and now<=max (true for the whole cacheTTL window) and returns the cached payload at line 271 without re-running verifyToken or any date validator. Because the date validators (lines 452-459) that check exp are only executed on a cache miss, an expired token remains accepted for up to cacheTTL after its exp. The patched version instead sets `expiresAt = Math.min(clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL, payload.exp*1000 + clockTolerance)`, bounding the entry by exp even without iat. Prerequisites: the opt-in `cache` option enabled (default off) and a token lacking iat; an attacker who obtains a short-lived token can keep replaying it after expiration. PoC (audit-root src/index.js): token signed with expiresIn:1000 and noTimestamp:true, verifier with cache:true, cacheTTL:600000 returned the payload when verified at t=0 and, after the 1.5s sleep, a second verification still returned the payload (cache hit) even though exp had passed, instead of raising FAST_JWT_EXPIRED.

finding.title: Array-valued claims bypass strict iss/sub/jti/nonce validation (any-match instead of exact match)
finding.evidence: validateClaimValues() at line 159 accepts a claim value whenever ANY element matches (`!values.some(v => allowed.some(a => a.test(v)))` -> throw). The same function is now used for the scalar single-value validators as well: line 226 routes every non-date, non-array claim to validateClaimValues, and the validators for jti (line 467), iss (line 475), sub (line 479) and nonce (line 483) are all registered WITHOUT `array: true`. The type guard validateClaimType (line 149) only checks the element types (`values.map(v => typeof v).some(t => t !== type)`), so an array of strings passes it even though these claims are supposed to be scalars. Consequently a token carrying e.g. {"iss":["https://attacker.example","https://trusted.example"]} (likewise sub/jti/nonce) is accepted as long as a single element equals an allowed value, instead of being rejected. The upstream implementation kept a separate validateClaimValues using `values.every(...)` for scalar claims and only used the any-match `values.some(...)` variant for genuinely array claims (aud); merging the two removed that restriction, so the allow-list for iss/sub/jti/nonce can be satisfied by a crafted array claim rather than the exact claim value.

finding.title: Double free / use-after-free in ThinVec::clear when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `clear()` runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) and only afterwards resets the length with `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). If any element's destructor panics while the slice is being dropped, the panic unwinds out of `clear()` before `set_len(0)` executes, so `self.len()` still reports the full (now partially freed) length. The ThinVec is then dropped again during unwinding (Drop at line 1912-1928 calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`), re-running destructors on elements whose owned heap data (String/Box/Vec/etc.) was already freed, producing a double free / use-after-free. The type is used entirely through safe APIs (push + clear), so no unsafe is required of the attacker; std's Vec::clear sets len=0 before dropping exactly to avoid this. Reactive-on element Drop panic + heap-owning element type is sufficient to obtain the UAF/ACE primitive described.

finding.title: Double free / use-after-free in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` moves the vector out with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` (line 2546), then sequentially frees the unconsumed elements via `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547) and only then resets the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If an element's Drop panics mid-way, the local `vec` is dropped during unwinding with its length still equal to the original length, so `ThinVec::drop` (line 1912) runs `drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the entire buffer including elements that were already freed by the panicking loop, causing a double free / use-after-free. Reachable from safe code: build a ThinVec of heap-owning elements where one element's Drop panics, call `into_iter()`, leave it partially consumed and let it drop (or drop the iterator directly). std::vec::IntoIter guards against this with a DropGuard; thin-vec has no such guard here.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear() is not panic-safe, leading to double drop of elements
finding.evidence: clear() (lines 1082-1087) drops all elements via `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) and only then resets the length with `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). If the destructor of any element panics, unwinding skips line 1085, so the buffer's stored len still counts elements that have already been destroyed. The vector is then itself dropped during unwinding (or cleared again by the caller), and `Drop for ThinVec` unconditionally re-runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (line 1917) over that same len, double-dropping already-freed elements (double free / use-after-free). This is reachable from entirely safe user code (e.g. a Vec of a type whose Drop panics, or a containing collection whose destructor panics); no guard/length-reset-on-unwind protection exists. Upstream thin-vec 0.2.16 fixed exactly this by resetting len from a DropGuard during unwinding.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop is not panic-safe, leading to double drop of elements
finding.evidence: In `drop_non_singleton` for IntoIter (lines 2544-2549) the vector is first moved out into a local `vec` (line 2546), then the remaining elements are dropped with `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547), and only afterwards is the length cleared with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If any remaining element's destructor panics, line 2548 is skipped and the local `vec` is dropped while unwinding; `Drop for ThinVec` then re-drops `vec[..]`, which includes both the elements that were just destroyed and the elements before `start` that were already yielded/moved out, causing a double free / use-after-free. Reachable from safe code: partially consume an `IntoIter` and drop it (or let it drop during unwinding) while a not-yet-yielded element's Drop panics; no protection guards the length reset. Upstream thin-vec 0.2.16 fixed this by clearing the length from a DropGuard.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear drops elements before resetting len, so a panicking Drop causes double free/UAF
finding.evidence: Reachable from 100% safe Rust: store heap-owning values whose Drop can panic (e.g. String/Box/Vec wrapper) and call ThinVec::clear(). clear() destroys every element with ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..]) on line 1084 and only afterwards resets the length via self.set_len(0) on line 1085. If any element's Drop panics during that pass (the panic propagates out of clear()), line 1085 is never executed, so the ThinVec header still reports the old length even though the elements have already been dropped/freed. During stack unwinding the container is dropped again: ThinVec::drop -> drop_non_singleton -> ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..]) (line 1917) walks the stale length and drops/frees the same elements a second time, i.e. double free and use-after-free of the element payload. The code installs no RAII guard around the drop pass; std's Vec::clear avoids this by zeroing the length before dropping the elements (or via a DropGuard), and the upstream fix for CVE-2026-6654 introduced exactly such a guard here.

finding.title: Panic in element Drop during IntoIter::drop leaves len stale and double-frees remaining elements
finding.evidence: Triggered by safe code that creates an iterator and lets it drop without exhausting it (e.g. let mut it = v.into_iter(); it.next(); then drop the iterator) where a remaining element's Drop impl panics. IntoIter::drop calls drop_non_singleton (line 2553), which moves the buffer out with mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new()) on line 2546 and then drops the not-yet-yielded elements with ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]) on line 2547, only afterwards resetting the length with vec.set_len_non_singleton(0) on line 2548. If a Drop panics, line 2548 is skipped, and the local `vec` is dropped during unwinding with its length still equal to the original len; ThinVec::drop -> drop_non_singleton then runs ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..]) over the same (already freed) elements, re-dropping and re-freeing them (double free / use-after-free). No DropGuard guards the length update before the fallible drop pass, unlike std::vec::IntoIter; the upstream fix for CVE-2026-6654 added such a guard here.

finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks causes undersized Argon2 work_area heap overflow and unchecked malloc NULL deref
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() copies the caller-supplied nb_blocks straight into config.nb_blocks (line 328) with no range check, then sizes the buffer as work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024) (line 345) and calls crypto_argon2(..., work_area, ...) (line 347). _validate_u32 is applied only to password/salt/key/ad lengths (lines 334-342), never to nb_blocks. The C header documents the contract 'memory hardness, >= 8 * nb_lanes' (monocypher.h:160), but the binding never enforces it. In monocypher.c:752-754 crypto_argon2 derives segment_size = config.nb_blocks/1/4 and lane_size = segment_size*4, then at monocypher.c:776-782 unconditionally writes two full 1024-byte blocks (blocks[0] and blocks[1]) regardless of that rounding. With nb_blocks in 1..7 the binding allocates only nb_blocks*1024 bytes (<2048), so crypto_argon2 writes up to 2048 bytes into a smaller heap chunk, giving a reachable heap out-of-bounds write (attacker/application controls the cost parameter directly). Independently, malloc's return is never checked: a large nb_blocks (e.g. 0xffffffff => ~4 TB) makes malloc fail and crypto_argon2 immediately dereferences the NULL work_area at monocypher.c:757/781, crashing the process. No lower-bound validation and no allocation-failure handling protect the sink.

finding.title: Missing length validation of fixed-size key/nonce/mac/signature buffers causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: signature_check(signature, public_key, message) forwards the caller-supplied buffers directly to crypto_eddsa_check(signature, public_key, message, len(message)) without validating signature==64 or public_key==32 (line 429); the C function unconditionally reads signature[0..63] and public_key[0..31] (monocypher.c:2331-2336). Because the extern parameters are declared as fixed-size arrays (lines 27-31, 35-37, 111), Cython lowers them to plain pointers and performs no length enforcement, so a short bytes object (e.g. b'') yields a 64/32-byte heap out-of-bounds read. The same root cause exists in lock()/unlock(), where key (32), nonce (24) and mac (16) are passed to crypto_aead_lock/crypto_aead_unlock (lines 181 and 199) with only message length supplied, and in key_exchange()/compute_key_exchange_public_key() (lines 362/375) whose 32-byte key arguments are unchecked. Contrast with the correctly validated siblings IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption.__init__ (lines 214-218) and elligator_map/rev/key_pair (lines 501/519/543), showing validation is inconsistently omitted rather than applied. Result is an attacker-triggerable out-of-bounds read / process crash from untrusted short inputs.

finding.title: ChunkedReader consumes the two bytes after each chunk without verifying they are CRLF, enabling HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
Attacker-controlled bytes arrive through h11.Connection.receive_data() and are dispatched to READERS[SEND_BODY]['chunked'] -> ChunkedReader.__call__. When a chunk's data is exhausted, line 197 sets self._bytes_to_discard = 2, asserting that the chunk framing terminates with CRLF, and lines 163-167 then extract those two peer-supplied bytes and blindly consume them (self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)) with no comparison against b'
' -- there is no validation between line 166 and 167 (the 0.16.0 fix instead keeps b'
' and raises LocalProtocolError('malformed chunk footer') when data != self._bytes_to_discard[:len(data)]). Verified locally against this tree (h11 0.14.0): the stream b'GET /one HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

5
AAAAAXX2
45
0

' is accepted, yielding Request(/one), Data(b'AAAAA'), Data(b'45'), EndOfMessage, whereas 0.16.0 raises RemoteProtocolError for the same bytes. Any intermediary (load balancer/proxy) whose chunked parser treats 'XX2' as chunk data or ends the message differently computes a different message boundary for identical bytes, i.e. classic request smuggling on the bytes following a chunk (GHSA-vqfr-h8mv-ghfj / CVE-2025-43859).

finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks in argon2i_32 causes undersized heap allocation and out-of-bounds write
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() takes a caller-controlled nb_blocks and passes it into crypto_argon2 with only the upper-bound helper _validate_u32 applied to password/salt/key/ad (lines 334-342), never to nb_blocks. The work area is sized as malloc((size_t)nb_blocks * 1024) at line 345, but monocypher.c:crypto_argon2 unconditionally writes the first two 1024-byte blocks for every lane (FOR_T(u32,l,0,nb_lanes){ FOR_T(u32,i,0,2){ ... load64_le_buf(blocks[l*lane_size+i].a, hash_area, 128); } }, monocypher.c lines ~773-782). For nb_blocks < 2 the allocation is smaller than the two blocks written (e.g. nb_blocks=1 allocates 1024 bytes but 2048 bytes are written), producing a heap out-of-bounds write. Monocypher also requires nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes, which is not enforced. The malloc result is additionally not checked for NULL (line 345 -> 347), so a large nb_blocks yields a NULL pointer passed to crypto_argon2.

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length copied into fixed 128-byte stack buffer
finding.evidence: blake2b(msg, key) forwards the caller-supplied key and its length directly: crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) (line 281); Blake2b.__init__ does the same at line 297 with no key-length validation. monocypher.c:crypto_blake2b_keyed_init declares 'u8 key_block[128] = {0};' and executes 'COPY(key_block, key, key_size);', i.e. memcpy of key_size bytes. Because the binding imposes no limit (BLAKE2 allows at most 64, and the stack buffer only tolerates 128), a call such as blake2b(b'data', b'A'*1000) or Blake2b(key=b'A'*1000) writes past key_block, corrupting the C stack with attacker-controlled bytes.

finding.title: Missing length validation for fixed-size inputs read by C (signature/public key/nonce/mac)
finding.evidence: signature_check(signature, public_key, message) passes signature and public_key straight to crypto_eddsa_check (line 429) without checking len(signature)==64 or len(public_key)==32. Cython converts the Python objects to raw uint8_t* pointers without any length enforcement (the prototypes at lines 27-152 treat arrays as plain pointers), so a peer-supplied truncated value (e.g. a 1-byte signature or public key) makes monocypher read up to 64/32 bytes past the end of the Python buffer (out-of-bounds read); the verification result can then act as a memory-disclosure oracle. The same missing-length pattern applies to lock/unlock (key 32 / nonce 24, lines 181, 199), compute_key_exchange_public_key (line 362) and key_exchange (their_public_key 32, line 375), contrasting with the explicit length checks present in IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption.__init__ (lines 214-218), elligator_map/elligator_rev/elligator_key_pair.

finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks causes a heap buffer overflow in argon2i_32
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() copies the caller-supplied nb_blocks straight into the Monocypher config (line 328, `config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks`) with no validation that it satisfies Monocypher's documented precondition `nb_blocks >= 8 * nb_lanes`, then sizes the heap work area from that same unvalidated value (line 345, `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024)`) and passes it to crypto_argon2 (line 347). Monocypher's crypto_argon2 unconditionally fills two full 1024-byte blocks per lane during initialization (`blocks[l * lane_size + i]`, i in 0..1, monocypher.c:776-783) and later uses `last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1`, so with the default nb_lanes=1 an attacker/application can call e.g. `monocypher.argon2i_32(1, 1, b'pw', b'salt')`: segment_size = nb_blocks/nb_lanes/4 = 0 and lane_size = 0, yet blocks[1] (bytes 1024..2047) is still written into a malloc block of only 1024 bytes, producing a heap out-of-bounds write of 1024 bytes (attacker-influenced content derived from password/salt); small values like 2-3 also leave future accesses (`last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1`) outside the allocation. Protections are absent: no range check on nb_blocks exists anywhere in the wrapper, and Monocypher has no internal bounds check in release builds. Upstream confirmed and fixed this in 4.0.2.7 by inserting `if config.nb_blocks < (config.nb_lanes * 8): raise ValueError(...)` in argon2i_32, and the fix commit is titled 'Added parameter validation to prevent possible heap buffer overflow in argon2i_32.'

finding.title: Out-of-range SHA256 block index yields all-zero hash for arbitrary input
finding.evidence: Caller-controlled `paddedInLength` (signal input, line 97) is tied to `inBlockIndex` by `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;` (lines 110-111). Nothing constrains `inBlockIndex` to [1, maxBlocks]; only `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength` is checked (bitLengthVerifier, lines 125-128). Passing a small negative length (e.g. `paddedInLength = 0`, or values -5..-1 modulo p) makes `inBlockIndex` be 0 or a small negative field element, so the index assigned at line 195 (`arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1`) becomes a value close to the field modulus p (e.g. p-1). ItemAtIndex then checks `index < maxArrayLen` via `LessThan(bitLength)` (array.circom lines 25-28), but LessThan assumes both operands fit in `bitLength` bits; it computes `in[0]+2^n-in[1]` modulo p, so for index=p-1 the wraparound makes the test pass. No `eqs[i]` matches, CalculateTotal sums zeros, and every output bit is 0. Thus a prover can produce a valid proof that the SHA256 digest of any input is the all-zero bit array, independent of `paddedIn`; the padded message is not committed to by the output.

finding.title: Same under-constrained block index in Sha256Partial forces zero output
finding.evidence: `Sha256Partial` repeats the flaw: attacker-controlled `paddedInLength` (input, line 219) is linked to `inBlockIndex` by `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;` (lines 233-234) with no lower-bound/range constraint beyond `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength` (bitLengthVerifier, lines 237-240). For a zero or small negative length, `inBlockIndex` is 0 or a small negative field element, so `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1;` (line 292) evaluates to a value near the field modulus p (e.g. p-1). ItemAtIndex's `LessThan(bitLength)` guard is unsound for such out-of-range operands due to modular wraparound, so the check `lessThan.out === 1` passes while `index` is outside [0, maxBlocks-1]; all IsEqual comparisons are false, the selected sum is 0, and the returned 256-bit hash is all zeros regardless of `paddedIn`/`preHash`. The `Sha256Bytes`/`Sha256BytesPartial` wrappers inherit this through their calls into these templates.

finding.title: Missing lower bound on paddedInLength lets inBlockIndex become 0, so the SHA256 selector is driven with index -1 and forces a false all-zero hash
finding.evidence: Input: paddedInLength is a prover-chosen signal input (line 19 / 97) reaching Sha256Bytes and Sha256General. Flow: line 110 `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9);` and line 111 `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;` derive the block count, but there is no lower-bound constraint (no `paddedInLength >= 512` and no `inBlockIndex >= 1`). Setting paddedInLength = 0 satisfies both the equality and the upper-bound check `bitLengthVerifier` (LessEqThan, lines 125-128), yielding inBlockIndex = 0. Sink: line 195 (and identically line 292 in Sha256Partial) `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1;` feeds index = -1 (field element p-1) into ItemAtIndex. Failed protection: array.circom lines 25-28 use `LessThan(bitLength)` as a range guard, but circomlib's `LessThan(n)` only constrains `in[0] + 2^n - in[1]` to n+1 bits; it does not constrain `in[0]` itself. With in[0] = p-1 the wrapped value is `2^n - maxBlocks - 1`, which is < 2^n (since the assert guarantees 2^n > maxArrayLen > maxBlocks), so bit n is 0 and `lessThan.out === 1` passes for the negative index. ItemAtIndex then finds no matching IsEqual (all eqs = 0), so calcTotal.sum and out[k] are constrained to 0 for all 256 output bits. I reproduced the field arithmetic for maxByteLength=64 (maxBitLength=512, maxBlocks=1, bitLength=2) and maxByteLength=256: index=p-1 passes the guard and selects 0, while a positive out-of-range index (maxBlocks) correctly fails. Consequence: a malicious prover can produce a valid proof whose SHA256 output is 0x00...00 (e.g. by passing byte length 0 through line 33), a statement that is false for real SHA-256, breaking the soundness/integrity of any downstream check that uses Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial/Sha256General.
